newsitem.title: USA: Colombian doctor on trial over patient's death.
newsitem.headline: Colombian doctor on trial over patient's death.

text.p: A Colombian physician went on trial Wednesday accused of first-degree murder after he gave high doses of pain-killing drugs to a terminal cancer patient in a Florida hospital.
In his opening statement before Judge Robert Pyle and the jury, prosecutor John Agueros said he would not delve into motive and he avoided the terms mercy killing and euthanasia.
Instead, he said he would show Dr. Ernesto Pinzon, 37, acted with premeditation to end the life of Rosario Gurrieri, a patient in the painful final stages of lung cancer.

Attorneys for Pinzon, who could spend the rest of his life in prison if convicted, called the case a politically motivated "travesty of justice" and said motive was key. They said their client was following the family's wishes that he ease Gurrieri's pain and suspended medications that would prolong his life.

Gurrieri, 70, checked in to the Highlands Medical Centre in Sebring, a small city in Florida's citrus belt, last Oct. 5 with lung cancer that had spread to his spine, liver and other vital organs. His attending physician had given him no more than two days to live.

Pinzon, the doctor on duty, put Gurrieri on a morphine pump that allowed him to administer the narcotic pain killer himself. The doctor went home but later a nurse called to say the dosage was not working and Gurrieri's family wanted stronger medication.

Pinzon ordered an injection of 10 mg of morphine. When the nurse balked at the high dosage, Pinzon returned to the hospital and gave the injections himself. Altogether he gave 120 mg of morphine and 10 mg of valium.
When the patient's heart began to race, Pinzon administered potassium chloride, a drug sometimes used in lethal injection executions. Gurrieri died soon after.
Pinzon told investigators he used the drug to slow the patient's heart. Prosecutors say he used it because the morphine had failed to kill Gurrieri and the potassium was meant to be a coup de grace.

Pinzon's attorney Jack Edmund said during a break that defence witnesses would say Pinzon's treatment was sound. "There may also have been a substantaial political misreading of the elements in this case," Edmund said.
Jerry Hill, Highlands County prosecutor, is seen as a possible Republican candidate for state attorney general.

As he entered the courtroom, Pinzon, who is free on a $100,000 bond, hugged his weeping mother, who came from San Juan, Puerto Rico, for the trial. "My mother is suffering. She is my whole life. I am suffering for her," he said.
The Colombian consul in Miami, Camilo Cano, told Reuters Colombian groups in the United States had joined together in an effort to raise the $500,000 Pinzon needed for his defence.

Cano said his government did not wish to interfere with the U.S. justice system but "this is nothing like other cases of euthanasia under judgment in the United States" -- an apparent reference to Dr. Jack Kevorkian, who is accused of carrying out a number of assisted suicides since 1990.
Gurrieri's daughter Celeste is scheduled to be the first prosecution witness.
